projects.title: Great Circles as Geodesics of the Sphere
projects.target:
On the round sphere SR2⊂ℝ3S_R^2\subset\mathbb R^3, R>0R>0, every nonconstant unit-speed geodesic traces a great circle. Conversely every unit-speed great-circle arc is a geodesic.

A great circle is the sphere’s intersection with a two-dimensional plane through the origin. A geodesic has zero covariant acceleration. This is an intrinsic condition: its ordinary three-dimensional acceleration need not be zero.
imports: for the induced metric, the Levi-Civita covariant derivative is the tangential projection of the ambient derivative; elementary linear ODE uniqueness; inner-product differentiation. Curves are C2C^{2}, parameterized by arc length s. Global shortest-path claims are outside this theorem.

nodes.title: Sphere and Speed Constraints
nodes.proof:
Let gamma(s) be a unit-speed geodesic. The sphere and speed conditions are

$$\langle\gamma,\gamma\rangle=R^2,\qquad\langle\gamma',\gamma'\rangle=1.$$

Differentiating the first once gives $\langle\gamma,\gamma'\rangle=0$, so velocity is tangent. Differentiating again gives

$$\langle\gamma,\gamma''\rangle=-\langle\gamma',\gamma'\rangle=-1.$$

These identities are valid along the whole curve.

nodes.title: Covariant Acceleration Becomes a Radial Equation
nodes.proof:
The geodesic condition says the tangential projection of gamma'' is zero. The normal line at gamma is spanned by gamma itself. Hence $\gamma''=\lambda(s)\gamma$. Taking inner products with gamma and using N1 gives $\lambda(s)R^2=-1$, so

$$\gamma''=-\frac1{R^2}\gamma.$$

This nonzero inward acceleration keeps a geodesic on the curved sphere while its intrinsic acceleration vanishes.

nodes.title: Solve and Identify the Great Circle
nodes.proof:
At s=0 choose initial point p and unit tangent v, so ||p||=R, ||v||=1, and p·v=0. The unique solution of N2's ODE with these data is

$$\gamma(s)=p\cos(s/R)+Rv\sin(s/R).$$

Its image stays in the fixed plane span(p,v), which passes through the origin. Writing e₁=p/R and e₂=v gives an orthonormal pair and

$$\gamma(s)=R\big(e_1\cos(s/R)+e_2\sin(s/R)\big).$$

It therefore traces a great-circle arc. Any other initial parameter value can be shifted to zero, so this covers every unit-speed geodesic locally and throughout its parameter interval by uniqueness.

projects.title: Hopf–Rinow Theorem
projects.target: For a connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary, prove equivalence of metric completeness, geodesic completeness, and compactness of every closed bounded subset. Deduce that metric completeness guarantees a minimizing geodesic between any two points.
imports:
The Riemannian distance is the infimum of piecewise smooth path lengths on a connected finite-dimensional smooth manifold without boundary. Import normal-neighborhood geometry and Gauss lemma: sufficiently small radial geodesics minimize length and small metric spheres are compact images of tangent spheres. Import local geodesic ODE existence/uniqueness and the no-corner lemma: a piecewise geodesic that realizes the distance is smooth at its joins (first variation shortens a nonzero corner). These local facts do not assert global completeness or global minimizer existence.

For the minimizing-direction construction fix p≠qp\ne q and write r=d(p,q)>0r=d(p,q)>0. When proving the implication from geodesic completeness, assume that condition directly; N1 is needed only to obtain it from metric completeness.

1. If γ is defined up to a finite right endpointb, d(γ(s),γ(t))≤|s−t| makes it Cauchy as t↑b.

4. Christoffel symbols are bounded, so the geodesic equation bounds coordinate acceleration.

5. Velocity is therefore Cauchy as t↑b and has a limitv.

6. Local ODE existence from(x,v) extends the solution pastb, and uniqueness matches it to the old solution.

7. A maximal finite endpoint is impossible; the same reasoning applies backwards and at any constant speed.
